title: Music for games
author: edoc422
selftext: what is the best ai music generation for games. I am looking for something that can make looping songs which does not seem to be a common feature.

comments.author: Lisarde13
comments.body: I use [https://artlist.io/](https://artlist.io/) because I only need a few sounds for abilities and it's cheaper than Suno, but in my opinion, Suno is the best for the music itself.

comments.author: lyeeedar
comments.body:
I've found nothing that does looping, you'll have to cut that yourself. There's tutorials online on doing that with audacity.

Of the offerings, I've found Suno to be the best for music. Though it is facing challenges from the music industry so it may not be around forever.

comments.author: Key-Internet-1665
comments.body: Looping is definitely one of the harder requirements.

comments.author: EC36339
comments.body:
Just don't.

There are two kinds of games:

1. Games that have great soundtracks
2. Games that you play while listening to music

AI isn't going to produce type 1, so make it type 2 and just don't have music.

replies.author: Mistafyed
replies.body: There are also royalty-free bangers for all sorts of genres and just want credit, in fact some of the AI creation may use them for reference. Having AI music would be a quick way to get me to uninstall and refund.

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
I don't really care about the tool that was used.

There is something that makes music sound bland and generic, I can't put my finger on what exactly it is (probably there is a word for it), and music made by humans can be like that, too, and usually is by default. I know because I'm not a musician, I'm really bad at music, and whenever I try to come up with a uniquely melody in my head, it has either that exact problem, or it sounds too similar to a well-known melody that everyone would recognize.

If I made music for a game, by hand, people would probably think it's AI generated.

Then think of some of the most iconic soundtracks of games and movies you know. They have one thing in common: A memorable theme that immediately identifies it, if not the whole franchise. And it often gets repeated across other songs in the same soundtrack.

I've done some counting, and it is often 5 or 7 recognizable notes. In some extreme cases, it is 3 or even 2.

Try it:
* The Witcher: 7 notes
* The Witcher 2 Assassins if Kings: 8 notes (but it works with the first 7)
* The Expanse: 3 notes, and it couldn't be more basic.
* Gothic: 5 notes (and Corvus Corax' version reduced it to 4)
* EVE Online: They had one memorable title theme back in 2007, the Revelations tune. 7 notes. Then they scrapped it. A missed opportunity. Jon Hallur is good, but his other music is either not memorable or not title theme material.
Elden Ring: 2 notes. Crazy, isn't it. And no, it doesn't require any specific chords to be recognizable. And every boss has their own recognizable theme.
Star Wars: There are at least 3 (the main theme, the Imperial March, the sad tune).

I don't have the music theory to explain this, but there is a pattern to it. And it is solvable without magic.

A lot of music theory is math. And AI is already good at music theory. I asked it once to add arpeggio chords to a simple melody (just playing around with a sfx synth I've hand-rolled for my game). The outcome was harmonic and matched the chord progression of the original.

It's likely the same situation as with shader programming or with large scale software engineering. If you vibe code, or vibe compose, you get slop. If you build composable parts and direct the composition, you can build something good with AI, faster, and also better, because you are faster and therefore have time to make ot better.

And I bet a lot of serious "AI musicians" (or just musicians who are not anti-AI) are already doing that.

replies.author: kytheon
replies.body: Same argument can be made for art. AI art looks better than shit art but worse than amazing art. So why use AI for art?

replies.author: EC36339
replies.body:
My argument was for not having music at all, not about what tool to use.

You can make a playable game without music.

You can't make a playable game without graphics.

(Before autistic Reddit comes out of the woodwork to lecture me: Yes, you can make a game with only sound and no visuals, and blind people might appreciate it. But if you went by the argumentation of that smartass above, a game would have neither visuals nor audio, and only Helen Keller could play it)
